People march in support of Salvadoran troops deployed in Haiti, in Port-au-Prince. [Clarens Siffroy/AFP]By AFPPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Thousands of Haitians have taken to the streets of Port-au-Prince to show support for soldiers from El Salvador, deployed by President Nayib Bukele to confront armed gangs that control large sections of the capital.
Protesters on Tuesday carried signs reading “Thank you, Bukele” and “Long live Bukele”.
Bukele has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti since late October, after four soldiers from El Salvador went missing during an operation by the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The latest Salvadoran deployment, although separate from the GSF, has been welcomed by Haitian authorities, who have long sought additional reinforcements to combat the gangs.
Bukele’s hardline crackdown on gangs in El Salvador has broad public support but has drawn accusations of human rights violations.
On November 10, he claimed to have destroyed the “headquarters” of one of Haiti’s main gangs, releasing video footage of a helicopter attack.
Since then, Salvadoran forces, backed by Haiti’s national police, have taken control of a football stadium in the capital.
On Tuesday, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all security forces in Haiti to prioritise the protection of civilians and to use lethal force only as a measure of last resort.
In the first 10 months of this year, the UN recorded 4,595 killings and 2,050 injuries linked to armed violence in Haiti.
Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, has faced a deepening political and security crisis, with gangs tightening their grip on the country through a campaign of violence marked by murder, kidnapping and rape. Advertisement Salvadoran preside...

British PM Andy Burnham and Indian PM Narendra Modi [Getty Images]By Usaid SiddiquiPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Delivering a lecture in November 2025, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke of the lingering legacy of British rule that the country suffered for two centuries. Though India gained independence in 1947, it still needed to “decolonise the mind,” he said, laying out a decade-long plan to achieve this goal.
But on Wednesday, almost exactly a year after those comments, Modi will host Prince William and his wife, Catherine, the Princess of Wales, in New Delhi, after they also visited Mumbai — playing street cricket alongside Indian legend Sachin Tendulkar to kick off a three-day visit to India.
Recommended Stories list of 1 itemlist 1 of 1India-UK trade deal comes into effect: What’s cheaper in each country now?end of list
The British royals, visiting India for the first time in a decade, are attending the Earthshot Prize ceremony, one of the most prestigious environmental awards in the world, founded by William.
Modi’s conversation with the royals is expected to focus on the deep bonds, past and present, between their nations — a reality that analysts say is more powerful than the rhetoric politicians turn to.
The prime minister’s residence is no longer on Race Course Road: Modi renamed the street Lok Kalyan Marg (Public Welfare Street in Sanskrit). Several landmarks and towns named after British colonial-era figures across the country have been renamed under Modi, as have the country’s British-era criminal and penal codes.

A Shan farmer in Thailand's Chiang Mai province irrigates her crops with groundwater instead of the river water amid increased rare earth and gold mining at the river’s source in Myanmar [File: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Thai government authorities have raced to provide clean water for more than 20,000 households in northern Thailand after unsafe levels of arsenic, linked to rare earth mining operations in Myanmar, were found in the water supply.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul late on Tuesday ordered government agencies to find alternative water sources and closely monitor tap water quality in the province of Chiang Rai, according to deputy government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana.

Tap water supplies to thousands of homes in 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times over the safe limit.
Government authorities also found arsenic contamination in untreated water from the Sai River, a tributary of the Mekong River, at 25 times the limit for drinking water.
Authorities have deployed two trucks to supply residents with clean drinking water, while the government is also considering alternative river water sources.

Widely regarded as one of the most skilful fighters of his generation, Linares won world titles in three weight divisions during a 21-year career [File: Reuters]By Anushe Engineer and AFPPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
United States immigration authorities confirmed on Tuesday that former Venezuelan world boxing champion Jorge Linares remained in custody and was facing deportation proceedings after being detained on Sunday.
The 41-year-old was arrested by US Border Patrol agents and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials at El Paso International Airport, US media reported, citing an ICE spokesperson describing him as “a foreign national in the country without legal immigration status, arriving from Venezuela”.
“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” ICE said in a statement on Tuesday.
Three-time world champion Linares had announced his detention in a social media post on Sunday.
“ICE has detained me in El Paso, Texas. This is crazy,” Linares wrote on X. He has not posted anything since.
Al Jazeera was able to confirm through ICE’s online Detainee Locator System that Linares was being held at the El Paso Processing Centre.
Lawyers for the boxer said on Tuesday that Linares was “authorised” to be in the US.
“Mr Linares is authorised to be in the United States and he has cooperated fully with immigration authorities,” law firm Wilner & O’Reilly said.
“We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time.
“We are confident in Mr Linares’s position and ask his fans, the press and the public for patience in the meantime.”

Dil Hossain, Alinnesa and their daughter Ishara outside their makeshift home in Cox's Bazaar, Bangladesh [Masum Billah/ Al Jazeera]By Masum BillahPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Cox’s Bazar/Dhaka, Bangladesh — When Dil Hossain and his wife, Alinnesa, fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State during the military crackdown on their Rohingya community in 2017, they carried their newborn daughter, Ishara, and ran for their lives.
Dil’s elderly parents could not escape and were killed as the family fled, along with several other relatives.
“We ran for our lives through mud, hills and water, with the baby tied to us,” Alinnesa recalls.
Nearly nine years later, Ishara is growing up in a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, far from the village where she was born. She has spent almost her entire life in exile. Her parents depend on humanitarian aid, which has declined sharply in recent years, and continue to wait for a chance to return home.
Now, the family is hoping the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will recognise the atrocities committed against the Rohingya. On Thursday, the highest court of the United Nations is due to deliver its judgement in a landmark genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.
The Gambia filed the case on November 11, 2019, alleging that Myanmar had violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through acts committed against the Rohingya by its military and other security forces.
The allegations concern the so-called “clearance operations” that began in 2016 and escalated in August 2017, which The Gambia says involved genocidal acts intended to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part. The case asks the ICJ to determine Myanmar’s responsibility as a state under the convention. Advertisement

Forensic experts claim Epstein was strangled to deathBy Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
A forensic expert has analysed autopsy records and photos that he believes suggest US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein was murdered rather than died by suicide.
Following a years-long investigation, Michael Freeman, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine, told the CBS News broadcaster that he had concluded that Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind, while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges in 2019.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3‘Release Epstein files’, protester interrupts JD Vance’s speechlist 2 of 3Meghan Markle’s father arrested in US over alleged child sex abuse photoslist 3 of 3Rep. Thomas Massie Forces a New Fight for Epstein Survivorsend of list
“The injuries that were documented by the medical examiner were not consistent with the suicidal hanging,” Freeman said on Monday.
“If you put it all together, it is most consistent with a homicidal strangulation from behind using a narrow knotted fabric ligature,” he added.
Epstein was found hanging in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York on August 10, 2019. An autopsy concluded that he had taken his own life.
His death has long been the subject of conspiracy theories, with some claiming he was killed over fears he would provide damning evidence linking prominent public figures to cases of sexual abuse, rape and paedophilia.
Security cameras outside Epstein’s cell were not working on the day of his death. A 2023 Department of Justice report concluded that the facility had longstanding problems with its cameras.
